---
title: Schema mutation
description: "Select, update, extend, delete, reset, and temporarily override nodes of a live model."
---

Schema evolution lets a trained model accept new inputs or learn additional
targets while reusing compatible learned state. This supports adaptation after
[pretraining](../learn/pretraining-and-fine-tuning.qmd) or an earlier supervised
fit; train and evaluate the changed model for its new task.

Use model methods to change a live schema. They validate the edit, rebuild the
runtime graph, and retain state-dictionary entries whose names, types, and
tensor shapes still match. An edit can therefore retain some learned state
while initializing incompatible parts anew.

Runtime resources can own their rebuild rules. Online vocabularies preserve
their grown storage, label IDs, and compatible learned rows across schema
edits. Storage is managed automatically, not configured through field options.
Changing Cluster bounds can reinitialize assignment columns while preserving
its vocabulary; changing embedding dimensions likewise resets incompatible weights.

## Select and update

Predicates combine with logical AND. Inspect selected addresses before making
a broad change. This example uses `model` from
[Add transaction history](../learn/add-transaction-history.qmd), whose `trxns`
collection includes earlier payments and the latest payment:

```python
import relflow as rf

amounts = rf.where("address") == rf.Address("trxns", "amount")
selected = model.select(amounts)
model.update(amounts, description="Transaction amount in account currency")
```

Selection is read-only and evaluates predicates against the current schema on
every call. Plain callables are accepted; `rf.predicate(func)` wraps one for
composition with `&`, `|`, or `~`.

Updates are strict by default: every matched node must support each supplied
option. Narrow the predicate rather than mixing unrelated
node types. `strict=False` permits partial application to supporting nodes;
an option supported by none of the selected nodes still raises.

`mask=False` removes the selected node's policies; `mask=True` makes every
retained occurrence an always-hidden reconstruction target. This is the
transaction-history model's policy for `/trxns/disputed`. Optional sampled or
conditional reconstruction belongs in the later
[masking guide](../concepts/masking-and-reconstruction.qmd). Use `description` for
notes and declared field options for configuration.

Batch-dependent widths need no schema mutation. To deliberately remove an
existing branch limit, clear its overflow policy in the same update:

```python
history = rf.where("address") == rf.Address("trxns")
model.update(history, length=None, overflow=None)
```

Changing only `length=None` while retaining `"head"`, `"tail"`, or `"error"`
is invalid and restores the previous schema and graph. See
[automatic lengths and limits](../datatypes/branch.qmd#automatic-lengths-and-limits).

## Make a temporary change

```python
prediction_data = rf.ArrowDataModule(
    predict="payments/history/requests.parquet",
)

with model.override(amounts, active=False):
    ablated = model.predict(datamodule=prediction_data, batch_size=256, devices=1)

ordinary = model.predict(datamodule=prediction_data, batch_size=256, devices=1)
```

`payments/history/requests.parquet` is an application-supplied Parquet file. Its `trxns`
records retain the inputs; the directly bound `disputed` target can be omitted
from every transaction. The data module reads the model's current schema for
each prediction loop. The context manager restores the previous schema
attributes, even on exit through an exception. It does not snapshot all
weights, vocabularies, or normalizers: compatible learned-state changes inside
the context remain. See [Evaluation](../learn/evaluation.qmd) for an ablation example.

## Change the tree or reinitialize state

| Method | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `extend(...)` | Add named children to exactly one selected branch. |
| `delete(...)` | Remove selected nodes and their descendant subtrees. |
| `reset(...)` | Keep the schema and reinitialize selected runtime modules. |

```python
transactions = rf.where("address") == rf.Address("trxns")
model.extend(transactions, card_present=rf.Boolean, country=rf.Category)
model.reset(rf.where("address") == rf.Address("trxns", "country"))
model.delete(rf.where("address") == rf.Address("trxns", "card_present"))
```

An extension accepts keyword children or a `fields` mapping, following the same
parent-owned naming rules as construction. Names must remain unique.
Prepare the added fields inside each transaction before the next data loop.
Deletion cannot remove the generated root or leave an invalid empty tree.
`reset(..., descendants=True)` includes a selected branch's subtree; resetting
a field discards its learned runtime state, including any owned vocabulary.

## Edit between loops

Mutation is prohibited during active forward, inference, and Lightning loops.
Change the model between complete operations. Avoid direct attribute edits that
bypass graph rebuilding.

Rebuilds replace runtime modules. After editing a trained model, prepare a data
module for the updated schema, including any added fields. Calling
`model.fit(updated_data, batch_size=128, learning_rate=1e-4, max_epochs=30)`
with that module starts fresh optimization on the current parameters. Supply
any scheduler for this new run. Custom optimizer instances must also bind the current parameters;
an old instance can refer to replaced modules. Existing data modules keep the
model reference and use its current schema; application caches and exported
artifacts remain your responsibility.

A failed update that cannot rebuild restores its previous schema and graph.
Successful changes clear compilation and cached output contracts. Call
`model.compile()` again if wanted, reevaluate the changed model, and save the
artifact you intend to use.

## Evidence for learned behavior

The mutation evidence start with trained models, evaluate immediately after an
edit, and measure adaptation separately:

- [Neutral edits](../evidence/mutations/neutral-edits-preserve-learning.py)
  check prediction, normalization, and vocabulary retention.
- [Adding a hidden target](../evidence/mutations/extend-prediction-target.py)
  checks immediate retention and learning with continuation and scratch controls.
- [Selective reset](../evidence/mutations/reset-prediction-target.py)
  checks localized loss and relearning of one hidden output.
- [Deactivation and restoration](../evidence/mutations/deactivate-and-restore-input.py)
  removes an informative input, then checks updates, override exits, and
  reactivation from an inactive checkpoint.
- [Deletion and adaptation](../evidence/mutations/delete-input-and-adapt.py)
  compares retraining with inactive, scratch, and continuation controls against
  the best prediction possible from the remaining information.

These experiments cover specific edits and synthetic tasks. Consult their
recorded outcomes: retaining state entries does not establish identical
predictions when a schema-derived computation changes.

Hidden targets never reach the encoder, so adding one no longer changes a
branch's capacity or shifts its siblings' positions; old predictions are
retained up to floating-point reassociation. The recorded added-target
experiment predates that change and still shows the earlier capacity shift
until it is re-run. The new output learns successfully during adaptation.
